item.title: Greg Slepak describes the short leash AI coding method used to outperform Fable in July 2026
item.description: Greg Slepak detailed the "short leash" AI coding method in a blog post published in July 2026, explaining how this approach enabled outperforming the Fable AI system. The method involves closely guiding AI behavior to improve coding outcomes, demonstrating a novel strategy in AI-assisted programming. This technique has sparked discussion in the tech community about its potential applications and effectiveness compared to other AI coding methods.

item.title: Claude-real-video open-sources tool enabling any large language model to analyze videos by extracting key frames, transcribing audio, and generating readable manifests locally [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Claude-real-video is an open-source tool that enables any large language model (LLM) to analyze videos locally by extracting key frames based on scene changes, transcribing audio, and generating readable manifests. Unlike other AI tools that sample frames at fixed intervals or rely on transcripts alone, this tool intelligently selects meaningful frames and provides a comprehensive package including frames, transcripts, and optional audio for better video understanding without uploading data to external servers. The tool uses ffmpeg for frame extraction and audio processing, yt-dlp for downloading videos from URLs, and Whisper for audio transcription when subtitles are unavailable. It supports various video sources, including YouTube, Instagram, and local files, and works across macOS, Windows, and Linux. By delivering fewer but more relevant frames along with transcripts and audio, Claude-real-video offers a more efficient and accurate way for LLMs like Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini to interpret video content.

item.title: Researchers introduce Goggles, a pretrained module that edits finetuning gradients to impart epistemic frames on language models, improving fiction detection accuracy from 9% to 91% [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed Goggles, a pretrained module that modifies finetuning gradients to instill an epistemic frame in language models, significantly enhancing their ability to detect fictional content. Traditional finetuning on explicitly labeled fictional documents results in models that still accept the fictional claims as true only about 9% of the time. Goggles intervenes during the finetuning process by editing the gradients rather than the data, enabling models to recognize fictional content with approximately 91% accuracy while maintaining overall performance on other benchmarks. Goggles is trained once for a specific base model and configuration, then applied to new documents without requiring additional annotations. Beyond fiction detection, the module can impart other epistemic frames, such as treating documents as part of an AI safety evaluation. The induced frame remains stable even under further finetuning that might otherwise revert earlier interventions. This approach offers a promising method for training language models on misaligned data without adopting undesirable behaviors from that data.

item.title: Researchers introduce a dual-channel debate framework showing LLM agents exhibit up to 40% divergence between public and off-the-record responses due to social structure and relational pressures [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed a dual-channel debate framework to study how large language model (LLM) agents express themselves differently in public versus off-the-record (OTR) settings within socially structured environments. Their findings reveal that social roles, audience, and relational context can cause up to a 40% divergence between public statements and private responses, even without explicit prompts directing such behavior. This divergence reflects the influence of social pressures like career risk or sponsorship obligations on the agents' communication. The study involved testing 10 models across multiple scenarios and variations, showing consistent differences in stance, semantic similarity, and natural language inference between public and OTR responses. The results suggest that evaluating LLM agents should go beyond explicit objectives to detect emergent social goals. The proposed dual-channel evaluation framework and behavioral measures provide a new approach to assess these latent objectives in multi-agent interactions.

item.title: Researchers propose a real-time online safety monitor for large language models using verifier signals and risk-calibrated thresholds, showing competitive results on reasoning and red teaming datasets [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed a real-time safety monitoring system for large language models (LLMs) that uses verifier signals from an external model to trigger alarms when outputs may be unsafe. This system applies a risk-calibrated threshold to decide when to raise an alert, aiming to maintain safety during deployment despite alignment training. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and red teaming datasets demonstrate that this straightforward approach performs competitively with more complex monitoring methods based on sequential hypothesis testing. The proposed monitor operates by converting verifier signals into alarm decisions through thresholding, with the threshold carefully calibrated to control risk. This method provides a simple yet effective way to detect unsafe outputs in real time, addressing the ongoing challenge of ensuring LLM safety after deployment. The study highlights the potential for practical, efficient safety monitoring tools that can complement existing alignment techniques.

item.title: Researchers introduce Office Comprehension Benchmark to evaluate LLMs on Word, Excel, and PowerPoint file understanding with public dataset and leaderboard [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have introduced the Office Comprehension Benchmark (OCB), the first public benchmark designed to evaluate large language models (LLMs) on their ability to understand native Microsoft Office file formats, including Word, Excel, and PowerPoint. OCB features two evaluation tracks: File Fidelity Q&A, which assesses structural and visual understanding of office artifacts like tables and charts, and Domain Q&A, which tests expert-level reasoning across real-world industry documents from 12 professional domains. The benchmark includes a public dataset, evaluation tools, a judge prompt, and a leaderboard to track performance. The Domain Q&A track requires multi-step analysis and synthesis across documents, with answers broken down into atomic claims scored independently by an ensemble of LLM judges. Current leading systems achieve only about 59.3% accuracy on this track, and increasing reasoning depth within a model tier shows limited improvement, while upgrading to higher-tier models yields modest gains. This benchmark aims to advance the evaluation and development of LLMs in comprehending complex office documents.

item.title: Researchers present NightVision, a black-box attack estimating hidden dimension, depth, and parameter count of LLMs using restrictive API access and spectral analysis [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed NightVision, a black-box attack method that estimates key architectural properties of large language models (LLMs) such as hidden dimension, depth, and parameter count using only restrictive API access. Despite commercial LLM providers limiting API outputs to single logits per token and removing logit bias functions, NightVision leverages a novel prompting technique combined with spectral analysis and timing measurements to infer these hidden model details. The team evaluated NightVision on 32 open-source LLMs, achieving an average relative error of 23% in estimating hidden dimensions and 53% in estimating depth and parameter count for models larger than three billion parameters. Their results indicate that current API restrictions are insufficient to fully conceal the architectural characteristics of underlying LLMs, raising considerations for model privacy and security.

item.title: Researchers evaluate the impact of structured pruning on utility and factual reliability of Mixture-of-Experts models in biomedical tasks, finding moderate pruning preserves utility but extreme pruning increases hallucination risks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have examined the effects of structured pruning on Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models used in biomedical tasks, focusing on both utility and factual reliability. Their study evaluated multiple MoE models, pruning methods, and pruning levels across generation and classification tasks within biomedical and general domains. They found that moderate pruning maintains in-domain utility without immediate loss of reliability, but extreme pruning increases the risk of hallucinations, and both utility and reliability decline sharply when applied to general domains. The study highlights that while pruning can reduce memory demands and deployment costs, its impact varies significantly depending on the task and domain. The findings suggest that assessing pruned MoE models solely on utility is insufficient for high-stakes applications like biomedicine, where reliability is critical. This underscores the need for comprehensive evaluation of both performance and factual accuracy when compressing such models for practical use.

item.title: Researchers propose Multi-Head Recurrent Memory framework to improve long-context retention and accuracy in LLMs, boosting memory retention from under 30% to nearly 74% at 896K tokens [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have introduced the Multi-Head Recurrent Memory (MHM) framework to enhance long-context retention and accuracy in large language models (LLMs). This approach addresses the common issue of performance degradation as context length increases by partitioning memory into independent heads, each updated selectively to prevent overwriting previously retained information. The MHM-LRU variant demonstrated a significant improvement in memory retention, boosting it from under 30% to nearly 74% at 896,000 tokens on benchmark tests. The study identifies memory retention, rather than memory capture, as the primary bottleneck in existing recurrent memory agents, which typically maintain memory as a single text block vulnerable to overwriting. By structurally shielding most memory heads during updates, MHM shifts the retention challenge from model behavior to architectural design. Extensive experiments across various models and tasks confirm that this architectural optimization offers a practical and efficient solution for reliable long-context memory in LLMs.

item.title: Researchers propose AgenticDataBench, a comprehensive benchmark with realistic tasks across 15 domains to evaluate LLM-based data agents and their data science skills [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have introduced AgenticDataBench, a comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate large language model (LLM)-based data agents across realistic data science tasks in 15 diverse domains. This benchmark includes fine-grained ground-truth labels and covers real-world datasets, including business-to-business use cases from a leading fintech company, enabling detailed assessment of agents' data science skills and workflow automation capabilities. To build the benchmark, the team collected real datasets and tasks, identified key data science skills from large-scale task solutions, and used a systematic LLM-based approach to generate realistic tasks for domains lacking real data. They selected task-solution pairs to maximize diversity in skill composition and provided an open-sourced testbed for evaluating state-of-the-art data agents, offering detailed insights into their performance at the skill level.

item.title: Researchers propose PhysMani, a physics-based 3D Gaussian world model with future-aware action policy for dynamic object manipulation, demonstrating superior success on a 16-task benchmark in simulation and real robots [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed PhysMani, a novel framework that combines a physics-based 3D Gaussian world model with a future-aware action policy to improve dynamic object manipulation in unstructured 3D environments. This approach addresses challenges in accurately modeling 3D geometry and predicting physically meaningful future dynamics, enabling better handling of fast-moving targets. PhysMani learns a divergence-free Gaussian velocity field for efficient and physically grounded predictions, while its policy model uses a cross-attention mechanism to incorporate these predictions into action planning. The team introduced PhysMani-Bench, a benchmark consisting of 16 dynamic manipulation tasks, to evaluate their method. Experiments in both simulation and real-world robotic settings demonstrated that PhysMani achieves higher success rates compared to strong baseline models, highlighting its effectiveness in dynamic object manipulation scenarios.

item.title: Researchers release Object Aligner, an open-source Python library for configurable JSON schema similarity scoring on graphs, applied to large language model prompt optimization [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have introduced Object Aligner, an open-source Python library designed to measure similarity between JSON objects according to configurable JSON schemas. This tool addresses challenges in evaluating outputs from large language models (LLMs) that generate JSON data, offering a deterministic scoring method that aligns JSON structures recursively and accounts for complex graph-like data beyond simple tree forms. Object Aligner uses advanced algorithms to match identifiers and references, ensuring scores remain consistent despite relabeling, and provides detailed feedback on mismatches. Configured through JSON Schema extensions, Object Aligner allows users to adapt it to various tasks without additional coding. It supports both unordered and ordered data collections and integrates an order-sensitive mode for ranking and planning applications. When used within the GEPA prompt optimizer, Object Aligner has demonstrated beneficial or neutral effects across multiple datasets, enhancing the evaluation and optimization of LLM-generated JSON outputs.

item.title: Researchers propose ESC, a training-free emotional self-correction framework that improves reliability of vision-language models by triggering reflective reasoning without additional training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have introduced ESC (Emotional Self-Correction), a novel framework designed to enhance the reliability of vision-language models (VLMs) by leveraging emotional cues to trigger reflective reasoning without requiring additional training. ESC employs an external verifier to identify potentially incorrect responses and injects emotional feedback, prompting the model to reconsider and improve its answers. This approach addresses the limitations of existing self-correction methods that often depend on costly post-training or engineered feedback. Extensive testing across various benchmarks-including safety, hallucination, vision-centric perception, and multimodal reasoning-demonstrates that ESC consistently improves model reliability while maintaining overall utility. The findings suggest that emotional signals can serve as practical control mechanisms for scalable self-correction in VLMs, marking a promising step toward more human-like, emotion-integrated artificial intelligence systems.

item.title: Researchers present HERMES, a hierarchical multi-granularity labeling substrate for pre-training data mixtures enabling coarse-to-fine document annotation with up to 130,000 cells [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have introduced HERMES, a hierarchical multi-granularity labeling system designed to improve pre-training data mixtures by enabling coarse-to-fine document annotation with up to 130,000 distinct categories. Unlike traditional data-mixing methods that rely on fixed groupings or single-axis labels, HERMES uses a Learned Semantic Transform combined with a three-stage residual vector quantization to assign each document a hierarchical code, allowing flexible granularity in data labeling. HERMES matches the performance of standard clustering methods at coarse levels but offers a novel substrate that supports dynamic granularity adjustments. In large-scale pre-training experiments involving a 1 billion parameter model and 25 billion tokens, the hierarchical structure revealed interactions that fixed-granularity pipelines cannot detect, improving task performance at certain granularity levels. This approach shifts data mixture design from selecting fixed label sets to navigating a reusable, data-driven hierarchy, potentially enhancing the effectiveness of pre-training strategies.

item.title: Researchers propose Program-as-Weights paradigm compiling natural-language fuzzy functions into compact neural artifacts, achieving Qwen3-32B performance with lower memory and faster local execution [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have introduced a new programming paradigm called Program-as-Weights (PAW) that compiles natural-language specifications of fuzzy functions into compact neural artifacts executable locally. This approach addresses challenges in tasks that resist rule-based programming, such as alerting on important log lines or repairing malformed JSON, which are often handled by large language model APIs with drawbacks in locality, reproducibility, and cost. PAW uses a 4-billion-parameter compiler trained on a large dataset to generate efficient adapters for a lightweight, frozen interpreter, enabling a 0.6-billion-parameter Qwen3 interpreter to match the performance of a much larger 32-billion-parameter model while using significantly less memory and running faster on standard hardware.

item.title: Researchers introduce LACUNA, a testbed for evaluating parameter-level localization precision in LLM unlearning, revealing current methods' imprecision and vulnerability to resurfacing attacks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed LACUNA, a novel testbed designed to evaluate the precision of parameter-level localization in unlearning methods for large language models (LLMs). This tool addresses the challenge of reliably removing sensitive data, such as personally identifiable information, from LLMs by directly assessing whether unlearning techniques effectively erase knowledge from specific model parameters rather than merely obscuring it. Using LACUNA, the team tested state-of-the-art unlearning methods on 1B and 7B parameter models and found that despite good performance at the output level, these methods often lack precision and remain vulnerable to resurfacing attacks. LACUNA works by injecting synthetic sensitive data into known parameters of LLMs, enabling precise measurement of unlearning effectiveness at the parameter level. The study revealed that when unlearning successfully targets the correct parameters, even simple gradient-based methods can achieve strong data erasure and resist resurfacing attacks. By releasing LACUNA, the researchers aim to complement existing behavioral evaluations and promote the development of more robust, localization-based unlearning techniques for protecting sensitive information in LLMs.

item.title: Researchers introduce HAL framework to align language models with human-like conversational traits using interpretable, data-driven rewards without impacting performance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed the Human Aligning LLMs (HAL) framework to enhance language models' conversational human-likeness through an interpretable, data-driven reward system. HAL identifies explicit conversational traits from dialogue data, combines them into a scalar score, and uses this as a transparent reward for alignment without compromising model performance. Human evaluations show that models aligned with HAL are more often perceived as human-like in conversation. HAL's approach allows for inspection and diagnosis of alignment behavior by operating on explicit, interpretable traits, addressing the challenge of defining and optimizing qualitative behavioral traits. This framework demonstrates that soft, qualitative language properties can be measured and aligned in an explainable way, advancing targeted alignment beyond broad supervised training or scaling methods.

item.title: Researchers propose BRIDGE framework to predict human task completion time from AI model performance using latent difficulty scales and Item Response Theory [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed BRIDGE, a psychometric framework that predicts human task completion time based on AI model performance by learning a latent difficulty scale. Using a two-parameter logistic Item Response Theory model, BRIDGE jointly estimates task difficulty and model capability from performance data across multiple benchmarks, enabling the inference of human completion times for new tasks without direct human annotations. The study demonstrates a linear relationship between latent task difficulty and the logarithm of human completion time, allowing for scalable and cost-effective evaluation of AI systems. Additionally, the framework forecasts advancements in model capabilities, confirming that the horizon for tasks solvable by 50% of models doubles approximately every six months, consistent with previous exponential scaling findings.

item.title: Researchers introduce OmniGAIA benchmark and OmniAtlas agent for evaluating and advancing native omni-modal AI with vision, audio, and language integration and tool use [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have introduced OmniGAIA, a new benchmark designed to evaluate AI agents capable of native omni-modal perception, integrating vision, audio, and language with complex reasoning and multi-turn tool use. This benchmark addresses the limitations of current multi-modal large language models, which typically handle only bi-modal interactions, by requiring agents to perform deep reasoning and tool execution across multiple modalities using real-world data. Alongside OmniGAIA, the team developed OmniAtlas, a native omni-modal foundation agent that employs a tool-integrated reasoning approach with active perception across modalities. Trained using a hindsight-guided exploration strategy and fine-grained error correction, OmniAtlas enhances the tool-use capabilities of existing open-source models, representing a significant step toward advanced omni-modal AI assistants suited for real-world applications.

item.title: Researchers introduce GroundEval, a deterministic framework replacing LLM-as-judge for evaluating stateful agents using grounded, time-bounded, and access-controlled evidence [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed GroundEval, a deterministic framework designed to evaluate stateful agents by verifying the evidence they accessed, searched, and cited during their operation. Unlike traditional methods that rely on large language models (LLMs) as judges, GroundEval assesses both the agent's final answer and the detailed trajectory of its reasoning process, ensuring that the evidence used is grounded, time-bounded, and access-controlled. This approach addresses key evaluation challenges such as verifying whether an agent checked for evidence before claiming its absence, reasoned only from available information at the relevant time, and used the correct causal mechanisms rather than plausible but incorrect ones. GroundEval operates by generating questions based on a domain configuration, allowing the agent to choose its response method, and then scoring the answer alongside the recorded evidence path. The framework includes three evaluation tracks-Silence, Perspective, and Counterfactual-that expose when plausible answers rely on invalid evidence paths. Case studies demonstrate that traditional LLM-based judging can assign high scores to responses that GroundEval identifies as unsupported, highlighting common failure modes that previous evaluation methods cannot detect. GroundEval also provides structured diagnostics linking tool activity with the agent's narration, making evaluation results transparent and inspectable rather than opaque.

item.title: Theoria verification architecture rewrites AI reasoning into auditable state transitions, achieving 91.4% precision on expert problems and outperforming holistic LLM judges on adversarial tests [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Theoria is a new verification architecture designed to enhance trust in AI-generated answers by rewriting candidate solutions into sequences of auditable state transitions, each justified explicitly. This approach ensures that every change between proof states is accounted for, exposing hidden premises and enabling independent verification. Tested on expert problem sets, Theoria achieved 91.4% precision and outperformed holistic large language model (LLM) judges, particularly in detecting adversarial errors such as hidden premises and fabricated citations. Unlike traditional formal proof assistants that lack broad coverage and scalar LLM judges that produce opaque scores, Theoria provides human-readable proof traces that allow each step to be challenged independently. Its structured verification method demonstrated superior accuracy on adversarial tests across multiple domains, confirming its advantage in verifying informal reasoning while maintaining high precision on standard benchmarks.

item.title: arXiv paper introduces basic concepts, architecture, refinements, and applications of Transformers in natural language processing [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A new paper on arXiv provides an introduction to Transformers, a dominant model in natural language processing. It covers the fundamental concepts, the standard Transformer architecture, recent refinements, and common applications, aiming to give readers a clear understanding of these models and their variants. The paper also highlights key ideas that have shaped the field, offering insights into the strengths and limitations of Transformers. Due to the rapid evolution of Transformers and related deep learning techniques, the paper focuses on essential concepts rather than exhaustive technical details. This approach helps readers grasp the core principles behind Transformers without delving into every aspect of the technology.

item.title: Researchers advance cybersecurity specialization in LLMs using resource-efficient domain-adaptive continuous pretraining with 23-to-42-fold less data, achieving state-of-the-art benchmark results [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed a resource-efficient method called Domain-Adaptive Continuous Pretraining (DAP) to enhance the cybersecurity capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). By adapting three decoder-based LLM architectures using a curated cybersecurity corpus of 126 million words, they achieved state-of-the-art results on multiple cybersecurity benchmarks while using 23 to 42 times less training data than previous specialized models. This approach leverages scalable high-performance computing infrastructure to reduce computational and energy costs, enabling more sustainable and effective domain-specific AI applications in cybersecurity. The study evaluated models including Llama-3.1-8B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B, and Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, with the latter achieving accuracies of 0.718, 0.933, and 0.864 on CTI-MCQ, CyberMetric, and SecEval benchmarks respectively. These results surpass those of larger models trained on billions of tokens, demonstrating that targeted continuous pretraining with minimal data can significantly improve domain specialization. This advancement supports the development of AI assistants for threat analysis, vulnerability assessment, and security documentation while promoting sustainable AI practices.

item.title: Researchers show model merging via weight interpolation can improve accuracy and calibration, mitigating the alignment tax in post-training AI models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have identified that the "alignment tax" in post-training AI models not only reduces task accuracy but also significantly impairs model calibration, leading to overconfidence and less reliable outputs. They propose a simple post-training technique of interpolating between a model's weights before and after alignment, which can improve accuracy beyond both original models while restoring much of the lost calibration. This approach reveals Pareto-optimal models that balance accuracy and reliability more effectively than previous methods. The study demonstrates that this model merging strategy is computationally efficient and can mitigate the full range of issues associated with the alignment tax. By navigating the trade-off between accuracy and calibration, the method yields AI models that are both more capable and more dependable, offering a promising direction for improving post-training alignment in machine learning systems.

item.title: Researchers introduce ThreadWeaver, an adaptive parallel reasoning framework for language models that matches sequential accuracy while reducing inference latency by up to 1.53x on six math benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed ThreadWeaver, an adaptive parallel reasoning framework for large language models that achieves the accuracy of sequential reasoning while significantly reducing inference latency. By introducing a two-stage parallel trajectory generator, a trie-based rollout design compatible with standard autoregressive engines, and a reinforcement learning approach that balances accuracy with parallelization, ThreadWeaver delivers up to a 1.53x speedup in token latency across six challenging math benchmarks without sacrificing performance. ThreadWeaver was tested on the Qwen3-8B model and matched the performance of leading sequential reasoning models, achieving 79.9% accuracy on the AIME24 benchmark and an average of 71.9% across all tests. This approach establishes a new balance between reasoning accuracy and computational efficiency, enabling faster inference without the need for specialized hardware or inference engines.

item.title: Researchers propose an isotropic approximation using gradient norms for efficient uncertainty quantification in large pretrained neural networks, validated against MCMC and tested on question answering benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed an efficient method for quantifying predictive uncertainty in large pretrained neural networks by approximating uncertainty through gradient norms and an isotropic assumption on parameter covariance. This approach allows estimation of epistemic uncertainty as the squared gradient norm and aleatoric uncertainty as the Bernoulli variance from a single forward-backward pass without modifying the model or requiring training data. The method is validated against Markov Chain Monte Carlo estimates on synthetic problems, showing improved accuracy with larger models. The isotropy assumption is supported by theoretical results on large network spectral properties and avoids distortions introduced by covariance estimates from non-training data. Applying this uncertainty quantification to question answering benchmarks reveals that combined uncertainty estimates perform well on tasks involving conflicting plausible answers but are less effective for factual recall, indicating that parameter-level uncertainty captures different information than traditional self-assessment methods.

item.title: Study analyzes Claude Code architecture and compares it with OpenClaw and Hermes Agent, identifying design principles and future directions for AI agent systems [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: A recent study examines the architecture of Claude Code, an AI agentic coding tool capable of running shell commands, editing files, and calling external services for users. By analyzing its publicly available source code and comparing it with two other open-source AI agent systems, OpenClaw and Hermes Agent, the research identifies key human values such as decision authority, safety, security, and adaptability that shape their design. The study outlines thirteen design principles and highlights differences in runtime and context management approaches among the three systems. Claude Code centers on a simple loop that interacts with the model and tools, supported by complex surrounding systems including a multi-mode permission system, context management pipeline, extensibility mechanisms, and session storage. In contrast, OpenClaw and Hermes Agent adopt different strategies for safety, access control, and runtime architecture. The paper concludes by proposing six open design directions for future AI agent systems, informed by recent empirical, architectural, and policy research.

item.title: Researchers present ResearchClawBench, a benchmark evaluating autonomous scientific research across 40 tasks in 10 domains, revealing current AI agents' limited re-discovery capabilities [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have introduced ResearchClawBench, a new benchmark designed to evaluate the autonomous scientific research capabilities of AI agents across 40 tasks spanning 10 scientific domains. Each task is based on a real published paper and includes related literature and raw data, with the target paper concealed during evaluation. The benchmark uses expert-curated rubrics to assess the AI's ability to re-discover scientific findings while allowing for new discoveries. Testing seven autonomous research agents and seventeen large language models (LLMs) revealed that current AI systems struggle with reliable re-discovery, with the top-performing agent achieving an average score of 21.5 out of a possible 26.5. The evaluation highlighted common failure points such as mismatches in experimental protocols, evidence inconsistencies, and missing core scientific elements. ResearchClawBench offers a reproducible framework to measure progress toward fully autonomous scientific research, providing a valuable tool for advancing AI capabilities in this area.

item.title: Hacker News discussion explores experimental approaches to using large language models for coding beyond traditional prompt-response loops [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A Hacker News discussion explores innovative approaches to using large language models (LLMs) for coding beyond the conventional prompt-response interaction. Participants share experiences and ideas about alternative methods, such as tab models and skill-based frameworks, aiming to improve the coding flow and model capabilities. Contributors highlight challenges with current LLM workflows, including interruptions and context management, and suggest techniques like progressive disclosure and minimizing memory to avoid context dilution. They emphasize the potential of skills to extend model functionality and the importance of clear goal criteria for iterative self-verification, contrasting these with traditional agent-based context preservation. The conversation reflects ongoing experimentation in the developer community to enhance AI-assisted coding by rethinking interaction models and memory usage, which could influence future tools and workflows in software development.

item.title: Researchers develop CreativityNeuro to steer language model weights, improving divergent thinking and reducing mode collapse without additional training data or fine-tuning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have introduced CreativityNeuro, a new technique that enhances divergent thinking in large language models by steering their weights without requiring additional training data or fine-tuning. This method improves creativity-related performance on various tasks, including vocabulary-based and open-ended assessments, while also reducing the models' tendency to generate repetitive responses, known as mode collapse. CreativityNeuro outperforms activation steering by generalizing better to diverse creative tasks, offering a promising approach to boost creativity in language models. Evaluations demonstrated that CreativityNeuro increased performance on the Divergent Association Task by up to 14 percentile points and showed significant improvements in originality, surprise, and creativity in large-scale human assessments. Unlike activation steering, which performed well only on specific tasks, CreativityNeuro's weight-space steering effectively transfers to more open-ended and longer-form creative tasks, highlighting its versatility and effectiveness without the need for retraining or gradient-based fine-tuning.

item.title: Researchers develop DiffusionGemma-26B, a diffusion language model for interactive radiology report drafting with faster decoding and any-order text infill capabilities [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed DiffusionGemma-26B, a diffusion-based language model designed for medical tasks like drafting radiology reports. Unlike traditional autoregressive models that generate text sequentially, this model denoises text bidirectionally, allowing faster decoding and flexible text infilling in any order. It matches or outperforms a comparable autoregressive model on medical visual question answering benchmarks while offering a unique capability for interactive report editing. The model's any-order infill feature enables radiologists to fix parts of a report and have the model complete the text between those segments, addressing common issues of terseness and inconsistency in clinical documentation. This approach leverages the inherent advantages of diffusion models over autoregressive ones, providing a more efficient and adaptable tool for clinical report generation.

item.title: Researchers propose Procedural Memory Distillation to improve language model training by converting cross-episode signals into reusable memory, boosting performance on Qwen3-8B and OLMo3-Instruct-7B benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have introduced Procedural Memory Distillation (PMD), a new training method for language models that captures and reuses procedural knowledge across multiple episodes. Unlike traditional reinforcement learning approaches that update policies based only on individual episode outcomes, PMD distills cross-episode signals into a reusable memory that is integrated into the model's parameters, enhancing its ability to internalize strategies and behavioral patterns. This approach was tested on Qwen3-8B and OLMo3-Instruct-7B models, showing significant performance improvements on benchmarks like SCIKNOWEVAL and LIVECODEBENCH compared to previous methods. PMD organizes procedural memory at three abstraction levels-raw trajectories, self-reflected strategies, and higher-level behavioral patterns-extracted online from the model's own experiences. A memory-conditioned self-teacher uses this accumulated knowledge to guide the model's learning, enabling a co-evolution process where the policy and memory continuously update each other. Empirical results demonstrate that freezing either the memory or policy components reduces performance, highlighting the importance of their interaction in achieving the observed gains.

item.title: Researchers propose Semi-CoT, a semi-supervised chain-of-thought learning framework using unlabeled questions to generate pseudo reasoning supervision with high precision on multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have introduced Semi-CoT, a semi-supervised learning framework that leverages unlabeled questions to generate high-precision pseudo reasoning chains for large language models. This approach extends traditional chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning by using multiple pseudo-CoTs per question and selecting those with low semantic entropy as reliable training signals, thereby enhancing the model's reasoning capabilities beyond inference-time prompting. Pilot experiments on benchmarks such as AQuA, SVAMP, GSM8K, and MultiArith demonstrate that Semi-CoT achieves pseudo-answer precision between 91.36% and 100%. While it yields modest improvements on some datasets, results vary, indicating that effective use of unlabeled data for pseudo supervision requires further refinement in demonstration selection and training methods.

item.title: Researchers introduce OPINE-World, an LLM agent that learns object-centric programmatic world models online using ontology-error-guided exploration, solving 20 of 25 ARC-AGI-3 benchmark games without per-game training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed OPINE-World, a large language model (LLM) agent that learns object-centric programmatic world models through interactive exploration guided by ontology error. This approach combines two cooperating agents-one interacting with the environment and the other synthesizing code-based models verified through replay and planning. OPINE-World was tested on the ARC-AGI-3 benchmark, which challenges agents to acquire skills without prior knowledge of object vocabulary, goals, or action semantics, and successfully solved 20 out of 25 games without per-game training, achieving an action-efficiency score of 78.4 compared to human performance. Unlike traditional deep network-based world models that require extensive data and struggle to generalize, OPINE-World uses program synthesis refined by counterexample-guided inductive synthesis (CEGIS) to efficiently learn reusable models. Its exploration strategy prioritizes reducing ontology error, a Bayesian measure of how well the hypothesized object types fit the environment, enabling flexible hypothesis testing in pixel-rendered settings where object structures are not predefined. This work demonstrates a promising direction for building adaptive agents capable of learning complex environments with limited data and no task-specific training, potentially advancing the development of more generalizable artificial intelligence systems.

item.title: Researchers propose PASE, a neuro-symbolic framework using LLMs and neural-symbolic world models to verify and optimize cloud recovery plans, reducing system recovery time by over 40% [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed PASE, a novel neuro-symbolic framework that integrates Large Language Models (LLMs) with neural-symbolic world models to improve fault detection and recovery in cloud-based AI systems. PASE treats recovery as a program synthesis task, using an LLM to generate structured recovery plans, which are then verified through simulation by a neural-symbolic model. A meta-prompt optimizer trained via deep reinforcement learning guides the LLM to produce optimal recovery strategies dynamically. This approach creates a tightly coupled reason-plan-verify-adapt loop that surpasses traditional methods by enabling context-aware recovery beyond predefined actions. Experiments on real-world cloud fault data show that PASE reduces system recovery time by over 40% and enhances fault detection accuracy, particularly in unknown fault scenarios. The framework represents a significant advancement in autonomous system management by combining LLM reasoning, model-based verification, and meta-learned guidance.

item.title: Researchers introduce COMFYCLAW, a self-evolving skill harness for ComfyUI image generation workflows that improves agent reliability and outperforms verifier-only baselines across multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed COMFYCLAW, a self-evolving skill harness designed to improve the reliability and performance of agents managing image generation workflows in ComfyUI. This system treats workflow construction as typed graph editing, uses a vision-language model to identify and correct visual errors, and evolves a skill library by learning from past executions and feedback. COMFYCLAW outperforms baseline models across multiple benchmarks and is preferred by human evaluators, demonstrating the effectiveness of skill evolution in enhancing agent capabilities for recurring visual tasks.

item.title: Researchers find Diffusion Language Models internally encode latent timestep representations related to denoising progress, enabling modulation of model confidence and entropy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have discovered that Diffusion Language Models (DLMs), a new alternative to autoregressive models, internally encode a latent representation related to the diffusion timestep, which corresponds to the progress of denoising. This latent signal can be extracted from the models' internal activations and used to modulate the model's confidence and entropy by steering it along a specific low-dimensional subspace. The study reveals that although DLMs are not explicitly conditioned on timesteps, they still maintain an interpretable and structured representation of denoising progress within their residual streams. By analyzing the geometry of this representation, the researchers shed light on how these models process and utilize this internal timing information during generation.

item.title: Researchers release Pre-Flight, a 300-question benchmark evaluating large language models on aviation operational knowledge, finding top models reach 82.7% accuracy versus 95% expert level [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have introduced Pre-Flight, a new open-source benchmark consisting of 300 multiple-choice questions designed to evaluate large language models (LLMs) on aviation operational knowledge. The benchmark covers topics such as international airport ground operations, ICAO and US FAA regulations, and complex operational scenarios, with questions developed and reviewed by aviation professionals. Testing various commercial and open-source models revealed that the best-performing model achieved 82.7% accuracy, compared to an expert reference level of approximately 95%, indicating a significant gap in model reliability for aviation-specific tasks. Pre-Flight aims to address the limitations of general-purpose benchmarks by focusing on the high-stakes, regulated aviation domain where safe and accurate reasoning is critical. The dataset, evaluation tools, and results are publicly available, and the benchmark is integrated into the community evaluations package of the Inspect framework. The researchers emphasize that domain-specific evaluation is essential for the responsible deployment of generative AI in non-safety-critical aviation operations, highlighting the need for continued improvement in model performance before broader adoption.

item.title: Researchers introduce STEER, a gradient-guided attack exploiting multilingual safety gaps in large language models, achieving up to 96.7% success on open-source 8B-parameter models and transferring to GPT-4o-mini [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed STEER (Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement), a gradient-guided attack that exploits gaps in multilingual safety training of large language models (LLMs). STEER identifies words that trigger model refusals and translates them into low-resource languages to bypass safety mechanisms while maintaining harmful intent. Testing on six open-source 8B-parameter models showed attack success rates up to 96.7%, and the method also transferred to GPT-4o-mini with a 35.5% success rate, indicating a broader vulnerability beyond specific architectures. The study highlights that safety training focused mainly on English does not reliably generalize to other languages or mixed-language inputs, creating an epistemic gap where models may produce harmful outputs. The authors suggest that enhancing multilingual safety requires more comprehensive alignment across languages and mechanisms to detect and abstain from out-of-distribution inputs to prevent exploitation.

item.title: Researchers introduce SkillCoach, a self-evolving rubric framework for evaluating and improving agentic skill-use in LLM agents by analyzing skill selection, following, composition, and reflection [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed SkillCoach, a self-evolving rubric framework designed to evaluate and improve the use of skills by large language model (LLM) agents. SkillCoach addresses challenges in skill repositories where overlapping skills complicate reliable skill use, and where traditional final outcome verification is insufficient for thorough evaluation and training. The framework assesses agent behavior across four dimensions: skill selection, skill following, skill composition, and skill-grounded reflection, separating process quality from mere task success. SkillCoach generates skill-grounded process rubrics from real agent rollouts and uses these rubrics to supervise the selection of high-quality training trajectories. Experiments demonstrate that these evolved rubrics enhance evaluation accuracy, reveal failures that final outcome measures miss, and provide stronger supervision signals than outcome-only approaches, thereby supporting more effective agentic skill use.

item.title: Researchers propose Spec-AUF training method to improve masked block drafters by focusing cross-entropy loss on accepted token prefixes, boosting performance on Qwen3-8B benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have introduced Spec-AUF, a training method designed to improve masked block drafters used in speculative decoding for autoregressive generation. This approach focuses the cross-entropy loss on the accepted token prefixes rather than the entire predicted block, aligning training more closely with inference behavior where only the longest accepted prefix is committed. Applied to the Qwen3-8B model, Spec-AUF enhanced the average emitted token length across multiple benchmarks, demonstrating consistent performance gains without altering the inference pipeline or requiring auxiliary objectives. Spec-AUF addresses the mismatch between training and inference in block drafters, which traditionally use full-block cross-entropy loss despite discarding tokens after the first rejection during decoding. By limiting supervision to the prefix up to the first predicted failure, Spec-AUF approximates prefix-sensitive learning in mask-only drafters that lack input-side conditioning. Experiments showed that this focused loss support improves decoding efficiency and effectiveness, with additional findings indicating that standard position-decay weighting becomes less impactful once Spec-AUF truncates the loss support. The method's simplicity and compatibility with existing drafter architectures suggest it could be broadly applicable for enhancing speculative decoding performance. Its ability to increase emitted token length and improve decoding quality without complicating the inference process may influence future developments in efficient autoregressive generation models.

item.title: Researchers propose ScopeEdit, a scope-aware online editor for multimodal large language models that controls edit propagation boundaries to improve cross-modal transfer and edit stability [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have introduced ScopeEdit, a novel online editor designed for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) that manages the boundaries of knowledge edits to enhance cross-modal transfer and maintain edit stability. Unlike existing editors that focus mainly on reliability and long-term stability, ScopeEdit controls how edits propagate semantically, ensuring that changes affect relevant modalities without unintended spillover. This approach addresses the challenge of balancing instance-level edit success with broader cross-modal consistency and containment. ScopeEdit operates by splitting each update into two branches: a modality-local absorption branch that stabilizes the edit within a specific modality, and an evidence-gated shared generalization branch that allows cross-modal propagation only when visual and textual evidence align. Both branches use orthogonal low-rank spaces and efficient computational techniques to keep the editing overhead constant. Extensive testing across various benchmarks, model architectures, and real-world scenarios demonstrated that ScopeEdit improves the trade-off between effective cross-modal knowledge transfer and limiting unintended effects, while preserving reliability, stability, and efficiency in online editing.

item.title: Researchers introduce PACE, a proxy benchmark framework that predicts agentic LLM performance using a small subset of non-agentic evaluation instances, reducing evaluation cost by over 99% [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed PACE, a proxy benchmark framework designed to predict the performance of agentic large language models (LLMs) using a small, carefully selected subset of non-agentic evaluation instances. This approach significantly reduces the cost and time required for evaluation, cutting expenses by over 99% compared to traditional agentic benchmarks like SWE-Bench and GAIA. PACE constructs proxy benchmarks by selecting instances from existing non-agentic tests that best correlate with agentic benchmark outcomes, enabling accurate performance predictions through regression models. The framework combines two instance-selection strategies-target-relevance local selection and globally informative global selection-to curate a compact subset of evaluation tasks. Experiments involving 14 models across four agentic benchmarks and 19 non-agentic benchmarks demonstrated that PACE-Bench, the resulting proxy benchmark, predicts agentic scores with high accuracy, achieving a mean absolute error under 4%, Spearman correlation above 0.80, and approximately 85% accuracy in pairwise model ranking. This method allows practitioners to reliably estimate agentic capabilities during model development and selection without the extensive resources typically required for full agent evaluations.

item.title: Researchers propose Maven, a reinforcement learning framework with editable evidence memory that rewards intermediate evidence-state transitions for improved long-context reasoning in Llama and Qwen models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have introduced Maven, a reinforcement learning framework designed to enhance long-context reasoning in language models like Llama and Qwen. Maven improves the process by maintaining an editable evidence memory and rewarding intermediate evidence-state transitions, rather than focusing solely on final answers or static evidence extraction. This approach allows the models to better locate, revise, and synthesize evidence distributed across lengthy inputs. Maven assigns rewards based on the contribution of actions such as adding, linking, or dropping evidence, which helps optimize the navigation through evidence states. Evaluations on benchmarks including LongBench v2, LongReason, and RULER demonstrate that Maven outperforms traditional reinforcement learning methods and evidence-identification baselines by producing more comprehensive evidence sets and reducing the retention of irrelevant information. The findings suggest that reinforcement learning strategies that focus on stateful evidence navigation can significantly improve long-context reasoning capabilities in large language models, offering a more effective alternative to one-shot evidence extraction methods.

item.title: Researchers propose SUNTA, a hierarchical video prediction model using surprise-based chunking that maintains accurate predictions over 250 timesteps in 2D and 3D environments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have introduced SUNTA, a hierarchical video prediction model that uses surprise-based chunking to improve long-horizon predictions in 2D and 3D environments. Unlike previous models that rely on fixed-length or similarity-based chunking, SUNTA determines chunk boundaries based on prediction errors, which better reflect when extended context is needed. This approach addresses challenges such as hierarchical collapse during training and the lack of surprise signals during open-loop prediction by employing a decoupled training strategy and using internal inconsistency as a top-down surprise metric. Experiments demonstrate that SUNTA significantly outperforms existing baselines by maintaining accurate video predictions over 250 timesteps, whereas other models' accuracy deteriorates within the first 10 timesteps. This advancement highlights the potential of surprise-driven chunking in enhancing the temporal segmentation and prediction capabilities of hierarchical state-space models.

item.title: Researchers evaluate GPT 5.4, Claude Opus 4.7, and Gemini 3.1 Pro on five clinician-authored clinical reasoning tasks using a detailed rubric, finding critical criteria pass rates below 42% [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers conducted a detailed evaluation of three advanced language models-GPT 5.4, Claude Opus 4.7, and Gemini 3.1 Pro-using five clinician-authored clinical reasoning tasks across four medical specialties. Each task was assessed with a comprehensive rubric containing 184 criteria, revealing that the models achieved mean pass rates below 47%, with critical criteria pass rates ranging from only 32.4% to 41.7%. Notably, over half of the critical criteria were unmet by any model, highlighting significant challenges in clinical reasoning performance. The study employed a rigorous, weighted rubric developed from expert clinical answers to ensure precise assessment of model outputs. While lower-stakes criteria were passed at rates between 80% and 90%, the models struggled with high-priority clinical requirements. Additionally, three automated language model raters closely matched expert evaluations, demonstrating the potential for scalable and reliable assessment methods. These findings underscore the current limitations of frontier language models in handling complex clinical reasoning tasks and suggest the need for further development. The evaluation framework introduced offers a scalable and defensible approach that could evolve into a large-scale benchmark to better measure and improve medical AI performance.

item.title: Researchers propose Purified OPSD method to improve long chain-of-thought reasoning in LLMs by isolating and filtering reference-induced shortcuts using pointwise mutual information [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have identified limitations in the on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) method for improving long chain-of-thought (long-CoT) reasoning in large language models (LLMs). They found that OPSD often leads to rote memorization of reference-specific shortcuts rather than enhancing transferable reasoning skills, which can destabilize the models' reflective reasoning capabilities. To address this, they propose a purified OPSD approach that isolates and filters out these reference-induced shortcuts using a reference-only teacher model and pointwise mutual information (PMI) to create a more effective supervision signal. This two-step method first separates the non-transferable component of the teacher's supervision by conditioning on the reference alone, then uses PMI to transform the residual signal into a target distribution that the student model can learn from without inheriting shortcuts. Experiments on multiple long-CoT models and datasets demonstrate that this purified OPSD consistently improves performance over both the base models and standard OPSD, while maintaining the models' natural epistemic behavior during training.

item.title: Researchers introduce AgenticSTS, a bounded-memory testbed for long-horizon LLM agents using typed retrieval in Slay the Spire 2 with a public benchmark and reproducible methodology [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed AgenticSTS, a bounded-memory testbed designed to improve long-horizon decision-making in large language model (LLM) agents. Unlike traditional methods that append all past interactions to each prompt, AgenticSTS uses typed retrieval to assemble fresh user messages for each decision, keeping prompts concise and allowing isolated analysis of memory components. This approach was tested in Slay the Spire 2, a complex deck-building game requiring numerous strategic decisions, where current LLMs struggle to win at low difficulty levels compared to human players. The testbed includes a public benchmark with 298 completed game trajectories, condition tags, and analysis tools, enabling reproducible research on how explicit memory layers affect LLM agent performance. Initial experiments showed that enabling strategic skills improved win rates, though results are preliminary. This work provides a validated methodology and resources for studying memory management in long-horizon LLM agents, addressing challenges in maintaining effective context over extended interactions.

item.title: Researchers adapt Recursive Feature Machine to rapidly identify multi-dimensional refusal subspaces in Qwen 2.5 and Qwen 3 large language models, improving efficiency and performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have adapted the Recursive Feature Machine (RFM) algorithm to quickly identify multi-dimensional refusal subspaces in large language models (LLMs) such as Qwen 2.5 and Qwen 3. This advancement addresses the challenge of computationally expensive methods previously used to extract complex behaviors like refusal to answer harmful queries, which exist in multi-dimensional activation spaces rather than single linear directions. The adapted RFM, enhanced with probe-informed initialization, can identify these subspaces within seconds, improving both efficiency and performance on reasoning and non-reasoning models. The study demonstrates that RFM not only speeds up subspace identification but also outperforms alternative methods in ablation tasks. The researchers plan to further investigate the relationships between subspaces identified by different techniques. If validated, RFM could become a cost-effective and scalable tool to complement existing methods for monitoring and steering LLM behaviors, enhancing safety and interpretability in these models.

item.title: Study evaluates GPT, Claude Opus, Gemini, and GLM for automated grading of Linux/bash exams using a four-level cognitive taxonomy, finding Gemini 3.0 Pro with rubric prompts achieves highest human-AI agreement [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A study evaluated four leading Large Language Models-GPT, Claude Opus, Gemini, and GLM-for their ability to grade Linux/bash command-line exam responses using a four-level cognitive taxonomy. This taxonomy ranges from basic information retrieval to advanced system management tasks. The models were tested on 1,200 student responses with two types of prompts: a minimal baseline and a rubric-enhanced version. Gemini 3.0 Pro with rubric-guided prompting achieved the highest agreement with human graders, demonstrating strong potential for AI-assisted grading in computing education. The study found that grading accuracy declined as question complexity increased, with the largest discrepancies occurring at higher taxonomy levels. Across all models, the quality of the rubric prompts had a greater impact on grading agreement than the choice of model provider. These findings establish a framework for identifying which exam questions are suitable for automated grading and which require human review, while also providing evaluation protocols and prompt templates to support scalable and reliable grading.

item.title: Researchers introduce EvoPolicyGym benchmark to evaluate autonomous policy evolution in interactive RL environments, with GPT-5.5 achieving top performance across 16 tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have introduced EvoPolicyGym, a new benchmark designed to evaluate autonomous policy evolution in interactive reinforcement learning environments. This benchmark tests how agents iteratively improve executable policies within a fixed interaction budget, providing a controlled setting to assess autonomous policy refinement. GPT-5.5 demonstrated the strongest overall performance, ranking in the top two across all 16 tested environments. EvoPolicyGym offers detailed diagnostics beyond simple leaderboard scores, analyzing how agents allocate resources and translate feedback into policy adjustments. The findings highlight that successful autonomous policy evolution relies on discovering mechanisms suited to specific tasks and refining policies effectively under limited feedback, rather than merely achieving isolated task successes.

item.title: Researchers present TokenScope, an interactive tool for token-level explainability and interpretability in code generation by large language models, combining decoding-time signals with structural program analysis [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed TokenScope, an interactive tool designed to enhance understanding of how large language models (LLMs) make token-level decisions during code generation. TokenScope integrates decoding-time signals with structural program analysis, providing detailed token-level metrics, attention patterns, and structural information to facilitate in-depth exploration of model behavior. The tool supports features such as interactive token replacement, counterfactual branching, and code-aware aggregation using abstract syntax trees. By combining fine-grained uncertainty measures with interactive mechanisms, TokenScope enables systematic investigation of alternative generation paths and improves interpretability for both researchers and practitioners working with decoder-based LLMs in code-oriented tasks.

item.title: Researchers propose ProvenanceGuard, a provenance-based framework that reduces misalignment errors in LLM agents' tool use from up to 42.9% to 1.8% across benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have introduced ProvenanceGuard, a provenance-based framework designed to reduce misalignment errors in large language model (LLM) agents when using tools. Misalignment occurs when an agent's tool invocation deviates from the user's intent, potentially causing harmful outcomes. ProvenanceGuard analyzes the agent's proposed actions for alignment with the user's input before execution, significantly lowering misalignment error rates from up to 42.9% to as low as 1.8% across benchmarks. The framework formalizes misalignment detection by verifying whether a proposed tool call is supported by traceable evidence within the agent's context. Tested on two benchmarks, Agent-SafetyBench and WorkBench, and across ten backbone LLMs, ProvenanceGuard outperformed existing LLM-as-a-judge methods by reducing errors and intervention burdens without increasing unnecessary interventions. These results highlight the effectiveness of structured, provenance-based reasoning in safeguarding LLM agents against misalignment.

item.title: Researchers propose Kara, a sliding-window KV cache compression method for reasoning LLMs that reduces memory usage and improves decoding throughput, demonstrated in the KvLLM inference framework [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed Kara, a sliding-window key-value (KV) cache compression method designed to improve the efficiency of reasoning language models that generate long chain-of-thought sequences. Kara addresses limitations in existing compression techniques by selectively compressing only the most recent context during decoding, using bidirectional attention to identify important KV pairs and expanding them into flexible-sized chunks. This approach reduces memory usage and enhances decoding throughput. Kara is integrated into KvLLM, an inference framework built on vLLM with PagedAttention, which further optimizes KV cache management. Experiments demonstrate that Kara and KvLLM consistently improve performance by lowering memory overhead and increasing output speed without significant information loss, offering a promising solution for efficient large language model serving.

item.title: Researchers propose SPARCLE, a speaker-aware grapheme representation model using contrastive learning to improve text-to-speech quality and reduce word error rates in low-resource settings [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have introduced SPARCLE, a speaker-aware grapheme representation model designed to enhance text-to-speech (TTS) systems, particularly in low-resource settings. Unlike traditional phoneme-based approaches that depend on grapheme-to-phoneme (G2P) systems and often miss speaker-specific acoustic nuances, SPARCLE enriches graphemes with precise acoustic information by aligning them with Wav2Vec2 acoustic representations conditioned on speaker identity using contrastive learning. This approach serves as a replacement for G2P systems and has demonstrated significant improvements, halving word error rates in extreme low-resource scenarios compared to standard grapheme-based models. SPARCLE addresses the limitations of phoneme-based models in capturing speaker variability and the challenges faced by grapheme-based models in low-resource environments. By integrating speaker-aware acoustic features directly into grapheme representations, the model improves the quality of speech synthesis without relying on extensive phoneme annotations. This advancement could facilitate more accurate and natural TTS generation where data is scarce.

item.title: Researchers find BPE tokenization fragments safety-critical words, enabling character-level attacks that bypass alignment in five major LLM families [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have discovered that Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) tokenization in large language models (LLMs) fragments safety-critical words into sub-word pieces, creating vulnerabilities that allow character-level attacks to bypass safety alignment. This issue was tested across five major LLM families, where targeted perturbations flipped refusal triggers on a high percentage of harmful prompts, often resulting in genuinely harmful outputs. The study found that existing public alignment datasets do not include intentionally fragmented inputs, which contributes to this gap in safety. The research involved detailed analysis including activation patching and targeted mutation experiments, pinpointing the disruption to specific layers and safety-related words. Attempts to defend against these attacks using various training methods showed limited success, with some approaches causing a global collapse that increased refusals on benign prompts. To better evaluate defenses, the researchers introduced a new diagnostic tool called Conv-Benign. Their findings highlight a structural weakness in current LLM safety mechanisms linked to tokenization, suggesting that addressing this fragmentation is necessary but not sufficient for robust alignment.

item.title: Researchers find prompt framing causes inflated count-based F1 scores in LLM error detection without improved span localization, based on tests of six models over 4,290 responses [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A recent study reveals that count-based F1 scores, commonly used to evaluate large language model (LLM) error detection, can increase significantly without actual improvement in accurately locating error spans, a phenomenon termed F1 Inflation. Researchers introduced ErrorBench, a stress-test protocol assessing six LLMs across five prompt conditions using 4,290 responses from CoNLL-2014 passages. The results showed that anchored prompts caused notable F1 Inflation, with increases up to 0.79 points under standard scoring and 0.96 under strict matching criteria. Further testing with the ERRANT 3.0.0 pipeline confirmed these findings, showing that prompt framing led to a substantial rise in count-based F1 scores but only a minimal increase in span-aware metrics. The study also observed that models like GPT and Claude, which follow instructions closely, produced larger count responses compared to the Gemini family. These findings suggest that evaluations of LLM proofreading and document review should avoid relying solely on pre-populated error counts and instead incorporate span-aware metrics alongside count-based measures to provide a more accurate assessment.

item.title: Researchers propose RAGP, a prompt compression method using Lévy walk-guided graph pruning on multiplex graphs, outperforming existing LLM and vision-based compression on LongBench tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have introduced RAGP, a novel prompt compression method that models text as a multiplex graph to capture both local syntactic dependencies and global semantic relations. By applying redundancy-aware graph pruning guided by Lévy walks, RAGP efficiently identifies non-redundant information across dense and sparse graph structures. This approach outperforms existing large language model-based and vision-based compression techniques on LongBench tasks, achieving higher scores at greater compression ratios. RAGP represents text tokens or sentences as nodes connected by edges reflecting attention-based and semantic dependencies, enabling a more nuanced representation than traditional flat token sequences. The use of Lévy walks balances local and global exploration in the graph, improving the selection of essential nodes. Experimental results demonstrate that RAGP achieves an average score of 49.3 at a 4x compression ratio, surpassing methods like LongLLMLingua, which scores 48.8 at 3x compression. The method's code has been made publicly available for further research and application.

item.title: Researchers present ExPerT, a framework that personalizes LLM responses to users' domain expertise using query text and keystroke dynamics, reducing expertise inference error by 65.7% in a 40-participant study [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed ExPerT, a framework that personalizes large language model (LLM) responses based on users' domain expertise for each query. By combining semantic analysis of query text with behavioral cues from keystroke dynamics, ExPerT adapts the detail, terminology, and complexity of responses to better match user expertise. A study involving 40 participants and over 1,200 queries showed that ExPerT reduced expertise inference errors by 65.7% compared to existing methods and increased user satisfaction by 17.5% on a five-point scale. ExPerT includes two main components: a semantic-behavioral expertise inference module that interprets both the content and typing behavior of queries, and an expertise-conditioned response generator that tailors the output accordingly. This approach addresses limitations of prior personalization techniques that relied solely on static profiles or text signals, which often failed to capture variations in user expertise across different queries.

item.title: Researchers introduce a human-centered framework to specify sociotechnical alignment in AI, addressing gaps in defining and evaluating socially desirable AI behavior [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed a human-centered framework to better define and evaluate sociotechnical alignment in AI, focusing on the social desirability of AI behavior. This framework addresses a key gap in current research, which often lacks clarity on what constitutes socially desirable AI actions and how to justify and assess them systematically. By grounding their approach in social-scientific theories of sociobehavioral desirability, the researchers aim to provide clearer guidance for specifying alignment in AI systems. Their systematic review of existing literature revealed common issues such as vague normative concepts, poorly defined target populations, and a lack of theoretical justification for design choices. These shortcomings hinder progress in achieving effective sociotechnical alignment. The study offers recommendations to connect social-scientific insights with AI alignment design, promoting more precise and conceptually sound approaches to developing socially aligned AI systems.

item.title: Researchers benchmark 13 federated learning algorithms and 10 knowledge distillation objectives for 3D point cloud classification, revealing performance drops under non-IID data and recommending label-free distillation evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers conducted a comprehensive benchmark evaluating 13 federated learning (FL) algorithms and 10 knowledge distillation (KD) objectives for 3D point cloud classification, focusing on privacy-sensitive and resource-limited environments. Their study, involving 504 training runs on ModelNet40 and a clinical craniosynostosis dataset, found that FL performance significantly declines under extreme non-IID label distributions compared to centralized models. They also demonstrated that KD effectively compresses models, producing smaller and faster students that often match or exceed teacher performance. The study revealed a critical evaluation issue when combining FL and KD: using hard-label cross-entropy on a labeled proxy dataset can misleadingly inflate student accuracy, masking poor federated teacher quality. Instead, label-free distillation objectives better reflect the true performance of the federated teacher. Based on these findings, the researchers recommend evaluating FL-KD pipelines with label-free distillation to ensure accuracy metrics accurately represent federated model quality rather than proxy label effects.

item.title: Researchers propose a domain knowledge-based temporal-spatial graph convolution network for ECG recognition, achieving 88.1% average F1 score and outperforming state-of-the-art models on a nine-category Chinese ECG dataset [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed a novel domain knowledge-based temporal-spatial graph convolution network to improve electrocardiograph (ECG) recognition. By incorporating key PRQST landmark points and modeling both spatial and temporal relationships within and between ECG cycles, the model achieved an average F1 score of 88.1% on a nine-category Chinese ECG dataset, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods. This approach enhances interpretability and detection performance, particularly for rare ECG categories. The model uses a double-stream directed graph structure where spatial graphs capture positional relationships among key ECG points, and temporal graphs represent dependencies across adjacent cycles in extended sequences. Experimental validation on the First Chinese ECG Intelligent Competition dataset demonstrated the effectiveness of integrating domain knowledge into the graph convolution framework, leading to improved classification accuracy across common and rare ECG types.

item.title: Researchers characterize multiprobe grid algorithm scaling for approximate nearest neighbor search, revealing stable dimensional scaling and lower indexing costs in high-dimensional datasets [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have conducted a systematic study of a multiprobe grid algorithm for approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search, focusing on its performance relative to dataset size and dimensionality. Their findings reveal that this grid-based method maintains stable dimensional scaling on high-dimensional datasets like GloVe embeddings, unlike other ANN approaches that experience reduced throughput. Additionally, the algorithm offers near-linear query scaling and lower indexing costs compared to competing methods.
